author: Nina Garcia Steel
title: Crossing Dimensions of Pain Without Losing My Soul
content:
A

s I sit here in my—as I like to call it—Oasis in the Desert, looking out my window at the morning clouds gloriously dancing to the tune the songbirds sing every morning is simply a treasure. I can smile at the sun and sway with the wind as it tickles my senses. I enjoy this morning view as I sip a cup of sweet herbal tea and take in the rays of light.




There was a time when such treasures were absent in my mind. I was living with undeniable pain that I could not explain, except in my poetry.




Photo by Nina Garcia Steel




It’s my heart that aches the most.




The feeling of nerves tearing and bones slowly breaking.




Flares of fire running through my veins.




The words that everyone took as metaphorical were literal words of agony from trauma that started decades earlier. It would take over half a century to discover the root cause of the autoimmune conditions that developed, the near dementia scares. At one point, I was having severe neurological attacks where I lost control of my limbs entirely, making them feel as though they were being tossed around like a rag doll. I picked three alcoholic husbands and stayed in abusive relationships. Little did I know that all of this was coming from the same place: 

unprocessed trauma

.




It took me by surprise too. I had been making decisions about who I chose to be my mate based on what I thought was normal from what

author: James Moore
title: Be More Human: Why Mental Health Care is Broken and What We Can Do to Fix It: An Interview with Sir Norman Lamb
content:
Hello, this is James and welcome to the Mad in America podcast. This week, we are asking why people with mental health conditions die 15-20 years earlier than people without. Why does the UK spend £100 million every year placing patients far from home? How did the question, ‘What matters to you?’ transform mental health care in Norway? Can mental healthcare be more compassionate?

Sir Norman Lamb asks these questions, and more, in his book Be More Human, published by Jessica Kingsley Publishers. Sir Norman is a former Health Minister, an NHS trust chair, and a dedicated mental health campaigner who was knighted in 2019 for his public and political service. He has seen the cracks in the system up close. In his book, he sets out to answer these questions, and many others, uncovering the reasons why our mental health services are failing. He shares eye-opening stories from patients who have been let down, but also inspiring tales from trailblazers who are shaking things up with creative, community-first solutions.

In this interview, we talk about how his personal and professional experiences led to him wanting to lift the lid on the UK’s mental health system. We also discuss how personal accounts of mistreatment and abuse motivated him to think differently about the human element so often missing from mental healthcare. Finally, we discuss novel, community-based alternatives that offer dignity, compassion and hope.

The transcript below has been edited for length and clarity. Listen to the audio of the interview here.

Norman Lamb: Thank you, James. You can drop the Sir bit. I’m happy just to be Norman, but it’s really good to talk to you; great that we’ve got this opportunity.

Lamb: Yes, it’s been an interesting journey, James, because if you scroll back to the late ’90s, early 2000s, I hadn’t really focused much on mental health. It hadn’t touched me in any particular way. Then I was elected to parliament in 2001, and as a member of parliament in North Norfolk, I wanted to be available to constituents to take up their concerns. I became aware of a lot of people coming to see me with their own stories about the mental health system and how, in their terms, they felt it was failing them in various ways: awful waiting lists, awful use of coercion and institutionalisation. Those stories leave a mark on you.

Then we were hit personally in our own family. Our oldest son, Archie, when he was 15, was diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder. We managed to get a referral to the Mental Health Trust at a moment when we were fairly desperate. He was in quite a bad way, and we were told that we would have to wait up to six months for anything to happen.

When you’re a family in despair and really anxious about a child, being told you’ve got to wait up to six months is sort of hopeless, really. I’m acutely conscious that for many people nowadays, it could be a year waiting. We did what any family would do if they’re able to. We paid for care, and in a way, there’s the injustice because most people can’t do that. They are literally just left waiting.

I sort of concluded that a service that leaves people waiting so long when they’re desperate is not really a service at all in any meaningful sense, and everyone preaches the importance of early intervention in mental health. Yet the system seemed to be delivering intervention at the latest possible moment, often when people were already in crisis.

Then scroll forward to 2012: I became a minister in the Department of Health, and you get a whole lot more stories, people coming to talk to you, wanting to influence you, and it’s a profound privilege for people to be willing to tell you their very personal stories. Sometimes about dreadful loss through suicide, but often just other failings of a system that is under acute strain, but failing too many people.

I left the department in 2015, after the General Election that year, and a couple of months after that, my elder sister, Catherine, who’d been in a state of acute depression after the death of our mother, made one or two attempts on her life and was admitted to a fairly dismal unit up in the north of England. She was in there for about 10 weeks. She was a voluntary patient. But despite being a voluntary patient, she was locked up with everybody else.

After her period in there, she was discharged back home. But some months later, she ended up taking her own life, and so our family had to cope with that tragedy, leaving two adult children who’d already lost their dad to bowel cancer. I suppose it left me thinking that a lot of money was spent on her. Those 10 weeks in an inpatient unit will have cost a lot of money. It’s effectively incarceration. But what good did it do? If someone loses their life after being discharged, and that’s an acutely risky period, we know that from data across the system, was there not a better way of using money to be more ambitious for someone?

In a way, it led me on a voyage of discovery to find more effective approaches that were more humane, kinder, more generous, more ambitious for people. That was in a period before I became Chair of the South London and Maudsley, which was in 2020. But the five years I had there sort of reinforced all of my views about a system that was under acute strain, despite enormous numbers of people doing their very best and often achieving amazing things, despite the system, not because of it.

So, this is not a criticism of people working in mental health. It’s a criticism of a systemic problem that I think has to be confronted. It’s sort of like a relic from a Victorian era that is too often cruel and inhuman, and should not be tolerated. We sort of end up tolerating the intolerable.

So, it’s a rather long answer, James, but that’s the story that led to me wanting to write a book to make my case, as it were, for change. I wanted it ultimately to be an optimistic, ambitious book. I offer a critique of a system that I think is failing. I enable people to tell their stories in the book about their experiences of the system, often harrowing and shocking. But then in part two of the book, I put the spotlight on a whole load of enlightened examples of beautiful practices and approaches that are humane, generous, kind, but also more effective at keeping people safe, and giving people the chance of a good life that the rest of us perhaps take for granted.

Lamb: Well, the book is in memory of Catherine, James, and I wanted it, in a way, to be a legacy for her. I want something good to come out of that tragic loss.

Lamb: Archie’s doing great, and that’s another important point I want to make, James, because I think often when young people experience mental distress or ill health, it’s easy for them to believe that this is almost like a life sentence, that their life will be defined by this. But actually, so often, there is an opportunity to get to a better place, to achieve some sort of recovery, to be able to enjoy life.

Archie is a good example of that. He’s now running a record label. He still experiences some anxiety, but he’s thriving as a human being, married with children. It’s a sort of success story, and there could be so many success stories. I suppose I want everybody involved in mental health, in whatever respect, whether it’s working in a service or whether it’s a family member, to actually have some hope and some optimism that not always, but so often, there are opportunities to enable people to get to a better place.

Lamb: I think it’s such an important point you make. I mean, before I get on to Birgit and the way she ran her service in Norway, I learned so much, doing the research for this book, discovering wonderful approaches like hers in Norway. But one thing that struck me when interviewing people who had their own experience of the mental health system was how people would describe how they’d been given one different diagnosis after another, and how disorienting and confusing that must be.

One amazing woman, Rai Waddingham, describes in her story this succession of different diagnoses. I asked her what that meant to her, and she said, well, it’s just the lens through which different people see me. But for the person concerned to be told one thing and then told another and then be given the label, perhaps of borderline personality disorder. They might suddenly discover that when you’ve got that label, the way you’re treated in the system gets worse because somehow you’re seen as a difficult person and somehow responsible yourself for your own actions, putting to one side or ignoring a life story which might get you to that place. You start to think this system is doing people damage, not helping them heal.

Now, it’s important to offer the caveat, as you did with diagnosis, that some people talk to me and they tell me that they’ve been really helped by the mental health system, often because they’ve been linked up with someone who really cares, who builds a relationship with them, and who aids their journey of healing. But for too many people, the story is one of trauma, and diagnosis is sometimes part of that experience.

Then you interview someone like Birgit Valla in Norway, and you hear that Birgit, from the inside, concludes early on in her career that the system isn’t working for the people she’s trying to help and that a different approach is needed. We really need to listen to those people who, from the inside, as a professional, are realising that something is not working. She sets up this service where she’s determined not to rush to diagnosis, not to rush to medication, but just to say, look, we’re here to help. Open the doors, ask people what matters to them, and build a relationship with people and jointly problem-solve.

I suppose what I’d say to you is if you can help resolve someone’s issues that are causing them acute distress and enable them to move on in their life without resorting to a diagnosis which can end up defining you, then surely, we can all agree that helping someone move on and rebuild their life after some joint work addressing the issues that are in their head or the causes of those issues that are in their head, surely that’s just a good thing. Can’t we all agree on that? Then when you hear from Birgit that in 10 years leading this service, she didn’t diagnose anyone. It’s just a wonderful example of how we can rethink how we do things.

And she had no waiting lists; we’ve become sort of conditioned in this country to believe that waiting lists are just an unfortunate necessity. They just are part of a system that’s overloaded with need. You then discover when you talk to people like Birgit, or you go to Trieste and you talk to the amazing Roberto Mezzina, that actually waiting lists are not necessary.

You can rethink things in a way that just enables people with open access to see someone immediately when they need help, not putting them on an awful, impersonal waiting list ignored for six months or a year or whatever it might be with potentially awful catastrophic consequences.

Lamb: The extraordinary thing, James, is that the Norwegian system gave people a right to a diagnosis. Now, I’m sure those people, those legislators who originally introduced that, were doing it for what they felt was a really good reason to ensure that people got help when they needed it and so forth. But, of course, that right to a diagnosis ended up with Birgit’s service facing potential closure because they weren’t routinely giving people a diagnosis.

She was faced with the loss of that amazing service until various parliamentarians stepped in late to save it, and new guidance was issued to allow it to continue, and now it’s spread to lots of places in Norway.

James, you’ll forgive me for trying to encourage people to get the book, but just reading the story about this, I mean, she calls it a help centre. That’s what they’ve become known as in Norway. I think people will find it absolutely fascinating, along with all of these other examples.

There’s a common thread that runs through almost all of the examples I give in part two, and that is the importance of relationships. If we stand back and think about it, this is not rocket science. We all, as human beings, are what our relationships are like. We are social beings, but we are ignoring the importance of relationships or treating someone as an island, separate from society, as psychiatry too often traditionally has done. I say that, being very clear that lots of psychiatrists have been very influential to me, people who completely get it and who recognise that their role is part of a much bigger picture.

Roberto Mezzina is a psychiatrist. He’s a wonderful human being who I have enormous respect for, a principled man. But the old-fashioned view of treating someone in isolation from the people that they have relationships with seems to me to be a flawed approach, and also treating them in a way where the professional keeps a professional distance from people. This is another thing that I found acutely fascinating. This principle spreads much further than mental health services.

There is a culture in a lot of public services that people working in the service have been sort of conditioned to believe that sometimes, for their own protection, they must keep a professional distance. Purposefully not establishing any sort of relationship with the person that they’re trying to help, keeping professional distance, not engaging, not getting to understand and know the person, not offering any vulnerability yourself. Actually, the very opposite of that is so much more helpful to the person seeking help, but actually also so much more rewarding for the professional.

Lamb: I’m glad you saw it in that light, and I think you’re totally right. The current system that I describe in part one is inflexible and not person-centred. I mean, we often use that expression, but it’s too often pretty meaningless.

I think another interesting aspect of the system, and this comes out in Liam’s story in the book—it’s an extraordinary story of someone who’d had a difficult childhood with a mother who experienced really significant mental ill health. Liam ends up in the mental health system, has such an awful traumatic experience that he literally escapes and gets abroad, gets away from the U.K. to escape the mental health system and lives an itinerant life in continental Europe for two or three years just to keep away from the system.

He returns because he’s heard, wrongly, I think probably you and I would agree, that a new generation of antidepressants may be more effective, and he wants to get hold of them to help him. He goes to see his GP, and he describes how he purposefully didn’t reveal to the GP what was going on in his head because he knew that if he did that he would be back into the system again, locked up in a dismal unit. What do we learn from that? We learn that we create incentives not to disclose, not to open up. Indeed, incentives to keep away from the system.

When you look at the disproportionate use of coercion in terms of the black community, you look at some of the horrific stories of lost life and damage to people in the Black community who’ve experienced the mental health system. The story told by Aji Lewis, who lost her son, Seni Lewis, a young Black student who lost his life after being admitted as a voluntary patient when he was in a bad place. He ends up with police being called to the unit on the first night there, restrained face down on the ground for half an hour by several police officers. There are echoes here of George Floyd. It happened before George Floyd, but he ends up a week later with a life support machine being switched off.

Now, when a community gets to hear of stories like that, what’s the incentive to engage with mental health services? Then we look at the data, and we know that Black teenagers are less likely to seek early help than their white counterparts. Well, is that surprising? I don’t think so. You then have a sort of loss of trust between the community and a mental health service, which is deeply unhelpful.

Then you compare it with Trieste in Northern Italy, where there’s a community mental health centre. Everyone knows where it is. The doors are open, long hours. There are six beds for anybody who’s worried about falling into a crisis. They can go there for a few days just to stabilise themselves in a kind therapeutic environment. But it’s the same people there, and there is continuity of support. There’s a friendly welcome, and anyone can go. You don’t need a referral from your GP. The contrast is enormous. What I found quite troubling was how a number of senior psychiatrists, including academic psychiatrists, would say to me, “Oh, Trieste works in Trieste, but it doesn’t work here.” Why is that? Have you been there? No.

A very different approach dismissed without properly examining it, without ever visiting or talking to the people there. I’ve been there three times now, and that sort of dismissive attitude is so much greater in London: we can’t do that here. Well, I would say in riposte that a young Black man in Lewisham has just the same right to be treated with dignity and respect as any person in Trieste in Italy. There are some universal principles at stake here about the way we treat human beings, which don’t depend on ethnicity or on location or on circumstance, but are universal, and we’ve lost sight of that. People who would often, I think, describe themselves as being progressive individuals end up in a position where they are refusing to contemplate change in a way that feels reactionary.

But what I found immensely positive at the Maudsley was that there were so many people who saw the need for change and then who embraced the opportunity to trial a new model of care based on the principles from Trieste and then found that attendances at A&E started to go down. Admissions to hospitals started to go down because this more humane approach was more effective for people.

Lamb: Well, I hope that this book will encourage people at the top in government. I’ve given a copy to the Minister responsible for mental health. I’ve given a copy to the Prime Minister. I would love government to lead the case for change. The centre of government in the U.K. can’t dictate a change of culture, but they can lead the conversation and encourage a change of culture within services and promote alternatives that might demonstrate much better outcomes. But at the same time they can encourage government to think afresh, and incidentally, James, to recognise that a different, more humane approach doesn’t cost more. If anything, it costs less than if you have a system that’s based very much on heavy medication and institutionalisation, and a lot of these inpatient wards are akin to being in prison. People have often described it to me as being like in prison or being incarcerated.

That costs a lot of money. We spend about 50% of our clinical budget in the NHS on inpatient care. That’s what it’s called, inpatient care. But in many respects, it’s akin to incarceration. Everybody in England is locked up, whether they’re voluntary patients or detained under the Mental Health Act. That in itself is really shocking, it seems to me.

The use of restraints remains endemic in the system, and you’re more likely, if you’re Black, to experience this sort of coercion. I want government to lead the charge on making the change, and they would see that they could achieve better outcomes for no more expenditure. You may have to spend some money on affecting the change, moving from one approach to another, investing in things like 24/7 community mental health centres. But you could do public-private collaborations and so on. But I also want a grassroots revolution. I want to get the message out to anybody who’s interested in mental health, as indeed we all ought to be, because every family is touched by it in some way or other.

I want to get the message out that we can all have an impact in our communities and in the organisations that we work in. We can all play a part in helping to prevent distress in the first place, because that’s one of the key themes in my book: that we pay so little attention to preventing distress. We allow people to fall into crisis, and then the system is overwhelmed. What a ridiculous way to behave. So much better, surely, to invest in preventing people from falling into distress in the first place. But I think every person working in a public service, not just in mental health services, who reads this book might reflect that they could do things differently.

I’m not claiming personal credit for this, because it was the editor who came up with the title of the book. I described my argument to him, and he said, “What about being more human?” I thought that encapsulated it perfectly. But you could almost describe it as a sort of call to our age, because in so many ways, we have an angry public space now and an enormous risk of an accelerating loss of humanity, and a reminder to everyone that we need to be more human to recognise the vital importance of human relationships and building trust between us in communities and in organisations. Then a grassroots revolution could change things fundamentally. I want change from the top down, but also from the bottom up.

Lamb: Well, thank you. I’ll join you in that shout-out to that community café, and what we need to remember is that there are thousands of those wonderful community-based groups all over the place doing this work. If the statutory formal service could learn from what is all around them, but so often ignored, then things could change radically.

Your description of the help that people get from engaging in those sorts of things reminds me also of Rai Waddingham. I’ve mentioned her before, but she describes this harrowing journey through the mental health system.

She’s someone who had very difficult experiences in childhood and teenage years, including abuse, and none of the things that happened to her in the mental health system really helped her. What actually helped her was this amazing thing called the Hearing Voices Network, where people who hear voices come together to engage with each other and to normalise the hearing of voices. They discover that you don’t necessarily have to eradicate the voice to move on and to start to enjoy life again. You can take back control, to coin a phrase from our political past in this country. The power of how she benefited from others with lived experience, after all of that specialist intervention, which had labelled her in different ways so unhelpfully, I thought that was incredibly powerful.

The only other aspect which we haven’t touched on is the fact that a lot of the same issues apply to people with a learning disability and people who have been diagnosed as autistic. Alexis’ story in the book is probably the most shocking of all.

As a minister between 2012 and 2015, I had to deal with the aftermath of a very shocking expose of abuse in a private hospital called Winterbourne View. The government response to that was to say that there are far too many people with a learning disability or who are autistic, or both, who are in institutional care. Some of these people are literally kept in solitary confinement, which surely is a human rights abuse. Some of them are fed through hatches in doorways.

We set a clear ambition that we should substantially reduce the number of people in institutional care. The shocking thing is that the numbers have come down, but they haven’t come down nearly far enough. Again, what we’ve recognised is that institutional care costs a lot of money, and we could be giving these people the chance of a good life in the community with support if we only had brave leadership.

I think it’s really important to recognise that a lot of the characteristics of our mental health system also end up having awful impacts on people with a learning disability and autistic people. Autistic people are often misunderstood in inpatient services, and Alexis’ story in part one of the book describes how the one thing that keeps her sane is running miles every day. She has to do this. Then she’s locked up in an inpatient unit. She can’t run because there’s no outside space, and this idea that the people who are acutely unwell for whatever reason are denied access to fresh air, to open space, to beauty and nature, I find just extraordinary. It’s a very stupid thing to do, and yet we routinely do it.

Even the old asylums that we rightly got rid of had access to open space. Today, we deny people even that in these units. It’s really important to recognise that this assault on people’s human rights applies also to people with a learning disability and to autistic people.

Lamb: Absolutely right, James. Thank you for everything you do on this podcast and more broadly on Mad in America and other countries’ equivalent systems. You’re giving a voice to people who are often not heard, and you’re exposing evidence that often is not seen or heard. You’re doing really important work, and I’m very grateful for it.

Thank you both for this inspirational podcast which restores hope that changes could be made which would be empathetic, compassionate and relationship-based. A further necessity is the urgent requirement to increase awareness of the tragic misdiagnosis of Common Psychotropic, Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) as ‘Serious Mental Illness’. Those who prescribe SSRI/SNRIs/ADs must do so with Fair, Full and Informed Consent. This must include warning patients, loved one/s and/or house-mates about AKATHISIA, with its increased risk of suicide. Prescribers MUST be competent in recognising, diagnosing and managing AKATHISIA. To see this misdiagnosed as ‘Serious Mental Illness – (eg ‘Psychotic Depression’ – ‘Bipolar Disorder’ et al) – makes mandatory accountability for misdiagnosis and its consequences seem entirely reasonable. What really shocks me now is that even community mental health sites have keypad controlled entry systems. I said to someone this just screams to the world that any psychiatric patient is potentially dangerous and was told that many reception staff have had issues with troublesome clients (this site had 2 or 3 in the pandemic, thats all I think) and they were frightened. And yet every single door in the waiting area is keypad controlled, reception people are behind glass and no doubt have a panic alarm if needed and yet the nhs trust chose to stop entry to everyone until they determined who you were. And yet hospitals, A&E depts, GP surgeries don’t do this. A&Es do have security staff but then they are far more likely to get problematic people turning up etc Frankly this kind of thing just confirms to the world that mh patients are mad and potentially dangerous. If reception staff are that scared why in earth are they working there in the first place? Sir Norman Lamb’s personal reflections on the UK’s mental health system highlight a painful truth: locking people away in Victorian-style institutions rarely leads to genuine healing. The story of his sister Catherine and the agonizing waiting lists for his son Archie expose how broken the current model truly is. Instead of relying solely on rigid labels and delayed crisis interventions, we need to align psychiatry with human dignity, early community support, and genuine compassion. Asking “What matters to you?” rather than just handing out diagnoses is the exact paradigm shift modern mental healthcare desperately needs. Report comment Reply

author: Marion Brown
title: A Decade of the Rise and Rise of “Functional Neurological Disorder” (FND)
content:
“FND occurs when the brain has difficulty sending and receiving signals properly, even though scans like MRI or CT appear normal. It affects movement, sensation, speech, cognition, and other functions. Symptoms are genuine, involuntary, and can be disabling.”




—

NIH website




M

ore and more people are being diagnosed with ‘functional neurological disorder’ (FND). FND is essentially a term for ‘unexplained’ symptoms—including severely disabling symptoms such as movement disorders, blackouts and so-called ‘non-epileptic seizures’—and which doctors say has no clear cause. I began to notice about 10 years ago that these ‘unexplained’ symptoms were the same symptoms as those experienced by some people when taking prescribed drugs for ‘depression’, ‘anxiety’, ‘stress’, etc. and especially when trying to reduce or come off these psychiatric drugs.




I began to meet more and more people with the FND diagnosis who were also experiencing withdrawal effects after stopping antidepressants, benzodiazepines, and other psychiatric drugs—but no doctors seemed to connect the two. author: Poetry Collection
title: Reality Kicks by Terese Blåklokke
content:
Learning the truth
can tear you apart
wrench your guts
and change 
	your heart

the solution is simple
but hard to complete
you must 
	let it rip
and reap the wheat

you must welcome 
	the actual
braincrunching fact
that the «experts» 
	you trust
are all part 
	of an act

they’re playing 
	their parts
as government tools
not knowing they too
are brainwashed 
	fools

«this poet is joking
she’s surely sarcastic»
you laugh 
	as your brain
turns more 
	into plastic




* * *




After over 20 years of battling the symptoms, Terese Blåklokke has overcome the struggles of her illness “schizoaffective disorder” through faith, art, poetry, food, intensive introspection and mental training. Today, when an official “expert” claims to present facts, she is quick to search elsewhere for the actual solutions – as that has been where she most often has found hers.

author: Justin Garson
title: Seeing BPD in a Positive Light: An Interview with Dr. Shay Welch
content:
P

eople often take psychiatric drugs because there’s something about themselves they don’t like—extreme low mood, threatening voices, or panic attacks. But many who’ve been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder (BPD) take drugs for the sake of others. They’re repeatedly told that their very personalities are disordered, pathological or just intolerable. This message is profoundly stigmatizing. It can contribute to isolation, loneliness, and even suicidal thoughts.




In September 2024, I talked with 

Dr. Shay Welch

, a philosophy professor at Spelman College. Welch, who’s been diagnosed with BPD, truly writes from an insider’s perspective—a perspective that’s nearly absent from the academic literature.




Shay Welch




Her recent paper, “

Am I Safe Enough for You Now? BPD and the Forced Erasure of Personal Identity

,” describes how people with BPD often feel forced to erase who they are to make others feel safe. We discuss ways of promoting more positive messaging around BPD, and creating a more tolerant and accepting society.




The title of her paper captures a theme that ran throughout our conversation: “treatment” for BPD is often less about alleviating the diagnosed person’s suffering than about making them more tolerable to other people. author: Anne-Marie Cicala
title: How My Body Rejected Lithium After 25 Years
content:
It was two o’clock in the morning on our first night out of town in New Orleans, and I woke up suddenly in the dark hotel room feeling horribly sick and needing to run to the bathroom. What ensued was messy and lasted for two hours. I kept waking up with my head in the toilet to do it again. I used most of the towels in the bathroom to clean up both myself and the mess I had made on the floor. At 4am, exhausted and beyond tired, not knowing exactly how to handle the situation, I opened my hotel room door completely naked, threw the armful of soiled towels into the hallway and went back to bed.

The next morning, I woke up extremely nauseous. I was thankful we had packed a decent amount of THC gummies, as they proved to be a savior for the next few days. The gummies took the nausea down to a level where I was able to function throughout the day, but I was still not feeling right or well. I didn’t know if it was from the previous night’s events, but I felt subdued by a heavy brain fog.

The day progressed slowly, as I was not feeling 100%, but I made it through, enduring other would just get a good night’s sleep and be better in the morning. Yet, without fail, I once more woke up in the middle of the night, more prepared this time, and got sick several times.

I really had no idea what was going on. Once again, I woke up with severe nausea but thought maybe a good breakfast would set me straight.

At the hotel restaurant, I could not tolerate the smell of the food. I could barely drink my coffee. My husband, looking at me searchingly, kept asking if I was okay. I tried to assure him that I would be fine, although I wasn’t sure I believed that myself. He finally said, “I don’t know what to do when my wife looks like she’s about to vomit at any moment.” Remembering how much the gummies had helped me the day before, I decided it was going to have to be another day like that, so I asked him to go up to the room to retrieve one for me. He happily obliged. I ate the gummy and was feeling relief within about 40 minutes. I could finally breathe and begin to perform as a person on vacation.

At restaurants, I noticed that the menus would shake furiously in my hands, as well as my fork and my drinking glass. I brushed it off as my usual lithium tremor combined with low blood sugar. I also noticed that my thirst was unquenchable. At one restaurant, as soon as the waiter set the water on the table, I chugged the glass immediately and instructed him to keep them coming, that I was extra thirsty. My husband looked at me with concern and kept the gummies coming, which were still keeping the nausea at a manageable level. My additional stomach ailments continued, but I pushed through them and tried to make the best of it, still under the spell of a heavy brain fog.

After another night of vomiting and immediately popping gummies as soon as I woke up, my husband and I put our heads together. We ran through the list of symptoms I had been experiencing, coming up clueless. Next, we thought back on anything that had changed recently. Aha! Indeed, my psychiatrist had increased my lithium right before we left for vacation.

Only knowing that connection, we began to research my symptoms plus the keyword ‘lithium’. Immediately, tons of links popped up about lithium toxicity, something neither one of us knew anything about. It seemed serious, but some of the stories I read seemed a lot graver than mine, so I figured I wasn’t in need of emergency care. I simply discontinued the lithium, and we went home the next day. Not getting back until later in the evening, it was the following day before I could go in for an emergency blood draw to check my lithium levels, something that had been done frequently throughout my nearly 25-year history of being on the medication.

I had been put on lithium for my early bipolar (then later schizoaffective) diagnosis when I was 18 years old, after spending the previous year psychiatrically hospitalized seven times for depression, anxiety, psychosis and unstable mood. I was promised mood stability and less suicidal ideation. It was supposedly the leading option, my best line of defense. That is what I was told for the next 25 years, but I was never told about lithium toxicity.

From the start, the side effects were horrible. So much GI distress and unquenchable thirst, which I know now was my kidneys urgently trying to rid my body of the essential poison of the drug. I learned to deal with it. Every now and then, during times of stability, my doctor would agree to let me discontinue it, but it never lasted more than six months. I had spent over half my life on lithium.

I knew from past experience that my lithium level usually landed around .7, a fine, therapeutic level. Once lithium is stopped, the levels decrease pretty quickly. So, after missing two days of medication, I was very surprised when my bloodwork came back with a level of 1.4. This meant it had to have been even higher in the preceding days. I did indeed have lithium toxicity. Being off the medication, I was already feeling better, so I really felt like if there had been an emergency, it had passed. And thankfully I happened to have an appointment with my psychiatrist that week.

I told her what happened and she was concerned, to say the least, left wondering why it happened. The increased thirst, I learned, was my body’s way of trying to flush the drug out of my kidneys. Since the emergency had passed, my psychiatrist had me do another blood draw, this time the levels amounting to .5, and decided it would be okay to restart the lithium at a reduced dose. Nothing else bad happened for several years.

Many say that lithium is a vile drug to the body. Others say that it is an excellent drug for the mentally ill mind. I would agree with both. It caused a terrible tremor that embarrassed me most of the time. It left me having to run to the bathroom within 10-15 minutes of eating, for years. I would have to plan ahead with Imodium for road trips, airplane rides, and even some social events. For a long time, I was drinking four 40-oz bottles of water a day, which of course left me always having to pee. However, it did seem to work for my mental health. I found it to be a good medication for suicidal ideation, something I deeply struggled with, as well as a stabilizer for my sometimes unmanageable mood swings. For these reasons, despite the physical aggravation, I stayed on the medication.

Fast forward three years later: one evening, about an hour after taking my nightly meds, I once again got very sick. I ran to the bathroom three or four times, purging a total of 20 times that night. My shaking was more pronounced than usual, and something just didn’t feel right. I hadn’t been this wrathfully sick since I had lithium toxicity three years prior. But there had been no increase in dosage, this time. Maybe this was just food poisoning? But deep down, I knew it felt different. I skipped my morning dose of lithium and went to the doctor that afternoon for another emergency blood draw.

My levels were fine at .6. I remained unconvinced, so I did not take my lithium for the next several days, during which I felt fine. I started thinking that maybe it had just been food poisoning after all, and that it was safe to restart the lithium since my levels did not point toward toxicity. I woke up and took my morning dose. Within the next few hours, my nausea began to grow more intense, which continued throughout the day, along with relentless diarrhea. After taking my nightly dose, I had to take a Zofran and crawl into the bed early.

The next day, I bravely took my lithium again first thing upon waking up, with my handful of other meds, and waited. The nausea began and I knew something wasn’t right. Shortly after, I threw up, but since I had not eaten, it was not as severe as the times before. It’s just not agreeing with me anymore, I thought, and made the decision to discontinue until I saw my psychiatrist two weeks later.

During the following two weeks, I experienced some emotional turmoil, but my body had never felt better. My bathroom habits resembled those of a normal person, my shaking had decreased some, I wasn’t guzzling as much water throughout the day, and I felt more clearheaded. As I finally sat down with my psychiatrist, I became very emotional about the whole ordeal. Historically, I felt that lithium had helped me more than hurt me, and with a tearful expression and cracking voice I said, “My body just doesn’t seem to be tolerating it anymore,” as I weepily described the events that had transpired in the previous weeks. Compassionately, she told me we could stay off the lithium for now. I was so relieved.

I have come to learn that in some cases, after long-term use of lithium, the kidneys’ ability to clear the drug changes, so the dose the body had handled for decades can become something it can no longer process the way it did before. I don’t know if I’ll ever be able to get back on lithium, but my mental state is stable and I am on another mood stabilizer, so I can’t complain. It was just a trip to have my body make a decision without me to cease a relationship I’d had with something for so long.

author: Donald Zrebiec
title: She Was Here: Finding My Grandmother After Willard
content:
I

 often mention that I was the only one of Catherine Smoral’s grandchildren to see her alive. I was six years old, and the visit to Willard State Hospital was a bad experience for all four of us who were there: my mother Anna, my Uncle Tony, me, and my grandmother Catherine. The three of us who came from Syracuse were all shocked at the physical and mental condition of our mother and grandmother. Our visit upset her, and we spent a very short time there before being asked to leave.




My grandmother was born in Poland in 1884. She emigrated to the U.S. in 1900, and in 1902 she married my grandfather, Karol Smoral. They were married at Sacred Heart, a beautiful Polish church that still stands on the west side of Syracuse. They were a happy couple who went on to have nine children, a happy and healthy brood. Karol bought his own home on Morgan Avenue, and a family burial plot at Sacred Heart Cemetery not far from it. In the early 1920s, disaster struck the household.




I received, I believe from Ancestry.com, a copy of an article from the Syracuse Herald from the early 1920s. This is how it read:




SMORAL FAMILY WOES CULMINATE IN COMMITTAL OF EIGHT TO INSTITUTIONS. Mother and Son Are Sent to Willard. Six Younger Children to Various Orphanages. Father Died in December.

Few people know that in Norway there is a society within a society, full of paradoxes and with no known way out. The Trial

, and what follows is a nightmare about the individual’s powerlessness against the arbitrariness of bureaucracy. Josef K. and Helen W. don’t have a great deal in common, since she walked out alive and victorious. Otherwise, the process was much the same.




“The media are failing their mission when they don’t raise this case to a systemic level. The practice itself is the problem, not whatever diagnosis the patient may have.”

author: Rupinder Legha, MD
title: From Eradicating Psychosis to Being With Voices: A Psychiatrist’s Journey from Biomedical Nihilism to Experiences of Humanity
content:
A

s a double-board-certified child, adolescent, and adult psychiatrist with nearly twenty years of experience treating “mental illness” worldwide, I have attended more mental health conferences than I can count. Nowhere is the tension higher than when the conversation turns to “schizophrenia” and “psychotic disorders.” Putting people with lived experience, family members of those labeled unwell, and clinicians in the same room for the sake of meaningful dialogue can sour fast. The purported goal of determining how best to support and assess a person can quickly shift to how to manage and control them. Someone inevitably insists there is no other way than meds and, if needed, forced “care.”




Four Conversations at Once




Amidst the cacophony, I sometimes have nothing to say, sensing that jumping in might only make things worse. The stakes always seem high for everyone in the room, the emotional charge palpable.




We might hear from people subjected to psychiatric coercion from childhood onward because of the voices they lived with, forced to submit to a construction of mental illness requiring involuntary hospitalizations and medications, and to culturally unsound formulations that pathologized them rather than looking for their meaning and value.

title: The Psychotherapist as a Paid “Fantasy-Friend”: The Taboo of Money and Payment in Therapy
content:
T

his text consists of a series of reflections that arose and developed from two events—one personal, the other relayed to me—concerning the act of payment in psychotherapy as well as the therapists’ own attitudes toward it.




The two incidents are the following:







My psychotherapist was quite clear and strict. Payment is made in cash at the end of the session—50 euros—and it’s best to have the exact amount. One day I had 60 euros (I can’t recall the reason for this “oversight” of mine), which obviously would have required her to give me 10 euros in change. At the time of payment, when I showed her the three 20-euro bills and told her that unfortunately I didn’t have the exact amount, I noticed an expression of obvious uneasiness on her face as she hurriedly opened her wallet and handed me the change for this transaction. This reaction struck me as particularly odd, as if she preferred to avoid such minor interactions in her psychotherapeutic practice.

During a session in a psychoanalytic training program, the training psychoanalyst noted that payment in psychotherapy is of the utmost importance and must always be required. author: Chandra Bozelko
title: I’m Done With Mental Health Providers
content:
B

ack in the early 2000s, my parents had me involuntarily hospitalized several times. I got the whole psychiatric smorgasbord: strapped to a gurney when I was perfectly able to walk, injected with medications against my will, 

spoken slowly and loudly to

 like I was incapacitated. I got the works, except for one hallmark experience of forcible treatment: I was never restrained because I didn’t do anything to endanger anyone. When people ask me why I didn’t kick or punch the nurse administering the shots, I don’t have a good answer. I’m just not good at violence.




The psychiatrists are, though. They never physically struck me — with all the damage they inflicted, they didn’t need to — but I saw one esteemed Yale shrink throw a red-haired woman onto a couch.




Because I criticized the system and I wouldn’t agree to debilitating regimens of medications, I was labeled as having no insight into my own illness. That’s worse than any diagnosis they can muster. To them, I was so ill that even the most severe psychiatric interventions would never help me. One famed Columbia doctor told my parents to abandon me, like leave me stranded there in New York, because I was terminally mentally ill.

author: Joanna Moncrieff, MD
title: The Fonagy Report: A Missed Opportunity to Challenge the Neurodevelopmental Narrative
content:
A

n independent review commissioned in the UK to address escalating demand for ADHD and autism diagnosis and treatment has missed an important opportunity to correct misleading notions about the meaning of psychiatric diagnosis and the nature and effectiveness of stimulant treatment.




The 

Independent Review into Prevalence and Support for Mental Health Conditions, ADHD and Autism

, led by Peter Fonagy, was published in mid-October.




It was 

commissioned to look at the causes of the rising demand for assessments for ADHD and autism

, sometimes referred to as neurodiversity, and to help people get the 

“right support”

. The truth is, the  UK’s National Health Service is buckling under the weight of this demand. Many adult mental health teams have had to stop accepting these referrals in order to continue to function. This means people are redirected to private providers at public expense. The report highlights how the NHS is overspending on these assessments by £164 million per year and the Centre for Health and the Public Interest describes the costs of this provision as 

“accelerating at an almost exponential rate”.

author: Peter C. Gøtzsche, MD
title: ADHD, a Unicorn in the Psychiatric (Be)wilderness
content:
A

ttention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder was invented in America and appeared in the American Psychiatric Association’s 1980 DSM-III diagnosis manual. But what is it?




At an NIH 1998 consensus conference, the chairman asked a leading ADHD expert, Mark Vonnegut, but he couldn’t explain what ADHD is:

1,2

 “They cannot sit still … they are difficult and they aggravate their parents … the diagnosis is a mess … I think, you know, we, uhm, I, I do, I think, part of the problem is that the profession keeps changing the diagnoses.”




Today, ADHD is a contagious, fashionable diagnosis.

3

 When youngsters look up descriptions of people who say they “have” ADHD on social media, they may be convinced they “have” it too and may even self-diagnose.




The diagnostic criteria for ADHD are so vague that when I lecture and ask people to try the adult ADHD test

4,5

6

 Many people are proud of their diagnosis and a British comedian said he needed to try the test five times before he passed.

author: Poetry Collection
title: Remembering That Day (Revised) by TJ Hamilton
content:
Pale days had long begun to stretch out


Until an effigy in motion forgot


About weeks and hours and better days


Without the tedious dinners for one.




The wife failed to see, as wives often do,


Frailties writ large across a husband’s heart,


Or maybe she’d believed since a little girl


In her man would beat a heart of steel.




Meanwhile,


To an unsouled effigy


It would all have been the same


To her, to me, and to all the others.




I might have persisted a while longer,


If I hadn’t had to decide,


How best to escape


The confusion of being a man.




Odysseus sacrificed to souls grown pale,


Bored with life in the world to come,


A drop of blood, an offering of life.


What else is an effigy to do?




* * *




Using “effigy” to represent depersonalization, and in this case depersonalization as a prelude to cutting my wrists, is courtesy of “Tranz” by Gorillaz.

author: Rob Wipond
title: A Biological Psychiatrist Wins the Nobel
content:
O

ne could be forgiven for feeling wary rather than celebratory this October when 

Stanford University neuroscientist and psychiatrist Karl Deisseroth

, along with two German scientists, 

received the Nobel Prize

 for inventing a new, invasive brain technology dubbed “optogenetics.”




After all, the last time a psychiatric treatment garnered a Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine was in 1949—for the lobotomy technique of severing the arteries into the brain’s frontal lobes. The award further boosted excitement among psychiatrists worldwide, who ultimately administered lobotomies to tens of thousands of people (often by, infamously, hammering an icepick through both eye sockets) as a “calming treatment” for hundreds of different mental and emotional conditions. Mainstream psychiatry later moved on from lobotomies with the emergence of new drugs. But 

protest campaigns

 led by family members of lobotomized patients continued for decades as they tried (in vain) to get the Nobel Foundation to rescind its award for a practice that had killed an estimated 5 percent of patients and left countless others permanently stripped of major emotional, mental, and functional capacities.




So, in 2026, is optogenetics biological psychiatry’s long-sought breakthrough for understanding and rectifying dysfunction in the mechanisms of the brain? Or is it another damaging, dangerous too

author: Matthew McWade
title: The False Promise of Patient Rights in Psychiatric Units
content:
I

 have been aware of patient rights since I began working as a Certified Peer Specialist in 2006. I had the privilege of serving as emcee at an M-POWERed event at the statehouse in 2009, and participated in testimony related to Massachusetts’ Restraint and Seclusion Initiative around the same time. I worked for a year at The Transformation Center, a wing of M-POWER, the now-defunct grassroots political organization that secured Massachusetts mental health patients their six fundamental rights on psych units. I knew each of the six fundamental rights by heart (humane environment, daily private visitors, professional communications, uncensored mail, phone access, and outdoor access), but after becoming a peer specialist, I rarely experienced psychiatric hospitalization myself and had little opportunity to see how well those rights were upheld.




During a manic episode in late 2025, I felt little fear about voluntarily admitting myself to my local psych hospital because I assumed my rights would be respected. After a single weekend, I was astonished by the poor implementation of the six fundamental rights, and my mental state deteriorated as a direct result of the psych unit’s inability to uphold even the most basic of those rights.

author: Ayurdhi Dhar, PhD
title: Being Mindful of Agony: How to Incorporate the Sublime in Our Daily Life—An Interview with Will Adams
content:
H

ow does a wounded world wound us in return? Can we be mindful and offer intimate attention to pain and trauma? We answer these and other questions with Will Adams who is an Associate Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology at Duquesne University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He holds a PhD in Clinical Psychology from Duquesne and completed his clinical psychology internship at McLean Hospital, affiliated with Harvard Medical School.




Dr. Adams is the author of 

A Wild and Sacred Call: Nature-Psyche-Spirit

, published by SUNY Press, a book that explores the deep connections between human psychology, the natural world, and spirituality. His work brings together phenomenology, relational psychoanalysis, Gestalt therapy, transpersonal psychology, and contemplative traditions, particularly Zen Buddhism and Christian mysticism.




His scholarship invites us to reconsider the relationship between self and world, mind and nature, and psychological healing and spiritual life. In this very personal interview, we’ll be speaking with him about how a lifetime of contemplative practice came to his rescue during the most traumatic time in his life, the possibilities of a relational understanding of human and more-than-human experience, and what psychology might learn from contemplative traditions and our relationship with the natural world.

author: Ekaterina Netchitailova, PhD
title: I Refuse to Die; I Am Not Leaving
content:
P

sychosis is treated like a crime, and the sentence is social death.




There is no place in society for people like me. I’ve known it deep down for a long time, but I was ashamed to say it out loud. Having had a psychosis is treated as worse than having committed a crime. Few experiences carry as much stigma, and the shame doesn’t fade when the psychosis does.




For more than twenty years after my first psychosis, I was barking up the wrong tree. I believed the main problem was that psychosis was misunderstood. I thought that, at least sometimes, it should be seen as a spiritual or religious experience that goes beyond medicine, and not simply as a mental illness. I spent years trying to prove that nothing was wrong with me, and that I could do not only as well as those we call ‘normal’, but even better.




On the surface, between my ‘psychoses’, I look like a successful, capable person. I have lived in four countries, speak four languages fluently, have a PhD, am raising my son on my own, and have a job I love. In reality, every day is a battle, and the weight of performing ‘normal’ threatens to pull me under. What I really need is a break, something like a stay in a Soteria house, where people can go through a crisis in a calm, homelike place instead of a hospital. But instead of resting, I always chose to carry on. I felt I had to show everyone that I am capable, smar

author: Patrick William Kelly
title: The Person They Never Asked About
content:
A

fter lights out at the state forensic hospital, a worker would peer through my door’s square window every fifteen minutes. He would quickly flick the overhead light on and off—just long enough to record whether I was breathing and in what position I was sleeping. Sometimes I could hear him whispering the data aloud to a partner making rounds alongside him, recounting our bodily orientations like buried bodies in a graveyard:




Left side. Right side. Back.




They knew the position in which my body slept every fifteen minutes for ten months. But they rarely asked me a personal question about my life.




I spent fourteen months in county jails and a state psychiatric hospital after accepting a not-guilty-by-reason-of-mental-disease plea on eight felony stalking charges arising from a psychotic manic episode. I had a doctorate from the University of Chicago and a book with Cambridge University Press. I had also been misdiagnosed by four different hospital systems, prescribed the wrong class of medications for four years, and carried an undetected neurosyphilis infection that inflamed my brain while every clinician I encountered looked somewhere else. author: Enrico Gnaulati, PhD
title: The Hidden Psychotherapy Drop-Out Crisis
content:
T

here is a psychotherapy drop-out crisis that the general public is largely unaware of and the mental health field apparently overlooks. 

Conservative estimates

 of the 

number of people who discontinue psychotherapy

 after starting hover around 28-33 percent, with well upwards of half doing so within the first few sessions. 

Trustworthy sources

 reveal that the 

median number of sessions

 received by people entering psychotherapy falls somewhere between seven and nine.




I call these estimates conservative because the way psychotherapy drop-out is typically defined and measured reflects medicalized models of short-term interventions aimed primarily at symptom reduction. 

Evidence-based treatment protocols

 considered adequate for improvement typically last 12-16 sessions, with 

a range of roughly 6 to 20 sessions

 depending on the type of disorder and its severity.




Admittedly, there are those people for whom a brief course of therapy aimed at symptom reduction is both preferred and satisfactory. However, it appears that such individuals are in the minority. 

A recent survey sponsored by the Psychotherapy Action Network (PsiAN)

 of more than 1500 adults in the U.S. found that 88 percent “Prefer therapy that may take longer because it helps you manage your symptoms and also addresses the root cause of problems.” Moreover, a substantial number of clients who

author: Richard Sears
title: Four New Studies Raise Concerns About Benzodiazepine-Related Harms
content:
T

his week, 

Mad in America

 examines four new studies around harms linked to benzodiazepine use. The first finds that benzodiazepines are linked to increased risk of heart failure and heart failure related hospitalization. The second reports that long-term benzodiazepine use (60 days or longer) is associated with worse cognitive function in people diagnosed with schizophrenia. The third finds that taking these drugs during pregnancy is linked to an increased risk of miscarriage. The fourth links benzodiazepines to increased risk of falls and fractures in older adults.







Benzodiazepines Linked to Increased Risk of Heart Failure




A new 

study

 published in 

Cardiovascular Toxicology

 finds that benzodiazepine use is linked to higher risk of heart failure and heart failure related hospitalization in people prescribed these drugs to treat insomnia. This research, led by Yi-Sin Huang from Taipei Medical University in Taiwan, also suggests that benzodiazepines are associated with a higher risk of heart failure hospitalization than other drugs used to treat insomnia.
